newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/mark suffers by U.S. close as EU bloc at odds.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark suffers by U.S. close as EU bloc at odds.

text.p: Dollar/mark suffered in U.S. trade as dealers placed bullish bets on the mark as evidence mounted on Monday that European Union members were at odds over the fiscal requirements for membership into a single currency, dealers said.

The dollar fell to a low of 1.7020 marks in U.S. trade, over four pfennigs below the 39-month high of 1.7423 marks reached on Friday, after dropping to a six-month low of 111.80 yen in Asian trade as nerves frayed ahead of Wednesday's scheduled release of fresh Japanese trade figures.
Dollar/yen recouped some of its overnight losses in quiet U.S. business to close higher at 112.90/00 yen from 112.45/50 at the open, but well below Friday's close of 114.33/43 yen.
The greenback fell to 1.7065/75 marks from 1.7125/35 marks at the open.

Dealers said Monday's price action was a continuation of a slide first sparked late on Friday when U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky reiterated recent comments from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin that Japan could not rely on exports to lift its economy out of recession.

"People are concerned about the Japanese current account numbers on Wednesday. They are expecting a further widening of the trade surplus that Japan has with the U.S. and people are buying yen on that," said Doug Lee, a corporate dealer at Sakura Bank Ltd.

Shaking the dollar from its perch against the mark was news that a meeting of European finance ministers on Monday failed to agree on final details of a stability pact aimed at ensuring spending discipline among countries to be joined in monetary union.

French Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told his European Union (EU) counterparts at a meeting in Luxembourg that the newly-formed French government needed more time to study the bloc's stability pact, an intergral part of its plans for economic and monetary union.

Foreign exchange markets have been in turmoil recently over whether Europe will meet the 1999 launch date for a single currency, to be called the euro, and whether the strict fiscal criteria required for membership will be weakened.

"The longer this goes on...without some sort of resolution or positive talk, the more people are getting a little bit wary of being short marks and they are starting to look at being long marks as an opportunity," said Elliott Dix, an assistant vice-president at Signet Bank in Richmond.
Strauss-Kahn said there would be further discussions with France's EU partners in the coming days, notably at a Franco-German summit in Poitiers in western France of Friday.
But asked whether he thought the EU could complete talks on the stability pact in time for a summit in Amsterdam on June 16-17, he said: "I don't believe we can complete it between now and then."
The Amsterdam summit had been expected to approve the pact which was largely agreed to by EU leaders at a Dublin summit last December.

Strauss-Kahn reassured the financial markets that the euro would be launched on time, but the dollar bottomed out against the mark after Bundesbank council member Raimut Jochimsen called for strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria for membership in monetary union.

Jochimsen said the need to maintain strict convergence criteria was greater than the need for a timely start, playing on dollar bulls' fears of a delay to the 1999 lauch date for the euro and strengthening the mark.

The dollar took little comfort in Rubin's off-stated remark that the United States favors a strong dollar. U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers also reiterated late on Monday that a strong dollar remains in the United States' interest.

In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.4370/80 Swiss francs from 1.4358/63 and to Canadian $1.3882/87 from C$1.3850/55. Sterling rose to $1.6368/78 from $1.6360/70. The Australian dollar rose to $0.7615/20 from $0.7609/14.
